terms.gloss: be excited, be beside oneself with joy; be itching to
terms.grammar: verb, fourth conjugation, intransitive: absolutely, with the ablative (laetitiā gestīre) or with an infinitive
evidence: Ter. Eun. 558: Chaerea, quid est quod sīc gestīs?
Cic. Fin. 2.14 (Lewis & Short): quōrum alter laetitiā gestiat, alter dolōre cruciētur
terms.comment: Properly, to throw oneself about with joy, as a child does (Festus, in Lewis & Short); with an infinitive, to be dying to do something (see be itching to). Cicero sometimes uses it of joy out of measure.

terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation, intransitive: with the ablative of the cause
evidence: Cic. Tusc. 5.16 (Lewis & Short): inānī laetitiā exsultāns et temere gestiēns
terms.comment: Literally to leap up, of horses and fish; of people, to leap for joy, and also to exult over someone or to boast (Lewis & Short).
Traupman’s word for “excited”, but in classical Latin it is any strong stirring of the mind, and most often agitation, alarm or upset (Lewis & Short; see affect). For happy excitement say gestiō.

phrases.latin: Chaerea, quid est quod sīc gestīs? quid sibi hic vestītus quaerit? Quid est quod laetus sīs?
phrases.english: Chaerea, why are you so excited? What’s the meaning of these clothes? What are you so happy about?

phrases.latin: ut aliquid scīre sē gaudeant? ut id aliīs narrāre gestiant?
phrases.english: how glad they are to know something, and how they long to tell it to others?

sources: Lewis & Short: gestio · Lewis & Short: exsulto · Lewis & Short: commotus
